Issue #19615 in scikit-learn/scikit-learn
Title: [RFC] Improve the Ridge solver speed / convergence tradeoff with better solver defaults
State: OPEN
Author: ogrisel
Comments: 15
Body: I did some follow-up work for the discussions on potential problems for Ridge(normalize=False) in #19426 and #17444 in the following gist:
https://gist.github.com/ogrisel/cf7ac8bca6725ec02d4cc8d03ce096a7
This gist compares the results between a minimal implementation of ridge with LBFGS  by @agramfort  against scikit-learn's Ridge(normalize=False, solver="cholesky"), Ridge(normalize=False, solver="lsqr"), Ridge(normalize=False, solver="svd") and other solvers.
The main conclusion is that those models seems to converge to the same solution, if we set a low value of tol and if we are not too strict on the tolerance: see how I defined atol in the gist. I cannot get convergence to machine precision (only around 1e-6/1e-7 in float64), but maybe this is expected. I am not so sure: I tried to tweak pgtol on top of factr but it did not improve.
On large-ish problems, L-BFGS can be significantly faster than our the always accurate svd solver (but not always, depends on the regularization) but never faster than the lsqr (LAPACK-based) solver. The cholesky solver (our default for dense data) is sometimes faster or slower than lsqr and L-BFGS (depending on regularization) but always faster than SVD (at least with high regularization). The sag/saga solvers are not necessarily as fast as they could be: I noticed that they do no benefit from multi-threading on a multicore machine, so that might be the reason. I have never seen then run faster than lsqr. sag/saga can be significantly faster than L-BFGS despite using fewer cores on problems with n_samples=5e3 / n_features=1e3 and not too much regularization (alpha=1e-6).
There are still problems with normalize=True as reported in #17444 but maybe we don't care so much because we are going to deprecate this option, see #17772 by @maikia that I plan to review soon.
Proposed plan of actions:

  proceed with the deprecation of normalize=True in #17772 and therefore put  #17444 on hold (or less of a priority) actually no, see: #19616.
 improve the ridge tests in scikit-learn by explicitly evaluating the min function for different solvers and maybe using a utility such as the check_min of my gist.
Tight tests (but without checking the minimum explicitly) #22910
 maybe add the ridge_bfgs function as a reference to compare against in our test suite? Since it does not seem to always converge to a very high quality optimum, I am not so sure of the value.
 maybe we could conduct a more systematic evaluation of various datasets with different shapes, conditioning and regularization to select  a better default than "cholesky" for dense data? "cholesky" is reputed to not be numerically stable, although I did not observe problems in my gist, maybe because of regularization. lsqr seems to be very promising, both in terms of speed and accuracy of the solution (according to my check_min thingy).
 I am not sure that our default value of tol=1e-3 is safe. It's probably very solver dependent, but I doubt that it's a good idea for the fast lsqr solver for instance (to be benchmarked if we do the above evaluation). #24465

Other ideas:

maybe we should consider adding l-bfgs an option? That would require doing more evaluation on sparse data / ill-conditioned data with various values of alpha. Not sure of the benefit compared to lsqr or cholesky though: they seem to always be more accurate than l-bfgs and faster (especially lsqr). And l-bfgs  can be very slow when alpha is small.
and maybe add a QR-based solver that is supposed to be more numerically stable? or is this what LAPACK is doing internally when we use the lsqr solver?
Comments:
[1] +1 for the plan except the "other ideas". I don't think that adding L-BFGS is necessary. And the QR based solver seems also an overkill.
for 2 you say lsqr for sparse case?
[2] for 2 you say lsqr for sparse case?

I am not sure what you mean. I edited the description to remove a previous version of item 2 because it was wrong (my tol was too lax and that was leading me to wrong conclusions).
[3] I'm also on board with the Proposed plan of actions, and, like @agramfort, don't think that adding lbfgs is necessary. A few further comments:

tol=1e-3 is indeed a bit large. On top, it means different things for different solvers.
"cholesky" solves the normal equations, i.e. computes X.T @ X + penalty, and therefore doubles the condition number of X which directly impacts the precision of solvers. The penalty should help, indeed.
You propose a QR based solution. I could imagine, solving [X, lambda*Identidy].T @ coef = [y, 0].T in some way could be interesting, as it avoids doubling the condition number.
lsmr is competing with lsqr. But in the past, I could not get a clear picture, which one to prefer in general.
Both first use a Golub-Kahan bidiagonalization and then Givens rotations (leading to a QR decomposition) and solving triangular linear systems is more or less all that is done.
lsqr should also work with sparse input and fit_intercept. If that were the case already, I could imagine to remove "sparse_cg".

…
[5] Also in my benchmarks, sparse_cg seemed to perform reasonably well, even on dense array data.
[6] @ogrisel Which benchmark are you referring to?

remove sparse_cg ? I would think it's the right thing to do for sparse X no?

Sorry, that suggestion of mine was typed too quickly and too late in the evening. I mixed up _solve_sparse_cg with cg based optimization routines. However, https://web.stanford.edu/group/SOL/software/lsqr/ states:

It [LSQR --Ed.] is algebraically equivalent to applying CG to the normal equation ( (A^T A + \lambda^2 I) x = A^T b, ) but has better numerical properties, especially if (A) is ill-conditioned.

On the corresponding LSMR page:

Special feature: Both (|r|) and (|A^T r|) decrease monotonically, where (r = b - Ax) is the current residual. For LSQR, only (|r|) is monotonic. LSQR is recommended for compatible systems (Ax=b), but on least-squares problems with loose stopping tolerances, LSMR may be able to terminate significantly sooner than LSQR.

[8] Regarding adding or not LBFGS as a solver to Ridge, I just came across a use-case to model a classic mechanical (based on Newton's second law) problem where weights of the linear model are expected to be positive. Right now, we allow adding positivity constraints in LinearRegression, Lasso, and ElasticNet. Ridge is the only lonely linear model that does not currently support this use-case.
If we would like to add support for such an option LBFGS might be the solver that we want to use for solving this type of problem. It would make our linear models consistent in this regard. Title: BUG log_loss renormalizes the predictions
State: CLOSED
Author: lorentzenchr
Comments: 13
Body: Describe the bug
log_loss(y_true, y_pred) renormalizes y_pred internally such that it sums to 1. This way, a really bad model, the predictions of which do not sum to 1, gets a better loss then it actually has.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
from scipy.special import xlogy
from sklearn.metrics import log_loss

y_true = [[0, 1]]
y_pred = [[0.2, 0.3]]

log_loss(y_true, y_pred)
Expected Results
-xlogy(y_true, y_pred).sum(axis=1)
Result: 1.2039728
Actual Results
Result: 0.5108256237659907
Versions
System:
    python: 3.9.14
   machine: macOS

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.1.2
Comments:
[1] can u share me the refernce of the code where the bug was there
[2] @TomDLT I'd be interested in you opinion. We hit this in #24365 (comment).
[3] I feel like computing a log loss with probabilities not summing to one does not make sense, so I am ok with the renormalization.

a really bad model, the predictions of which do not sum to 1

To me this is not a bad model (a model that has poor prediction accuracy), this is an incorrect model (a model that does not return results in the expected format), as would be a model that predicts negative probabilities. We could almost raise an error if the probabilities do not sum to one (or close), but I feel like it is simpler to just renormalize and compute the loss.
[4] I feel like computing a log loss with probabilities not summing to one does not make sense, so I am ok with the renormalization.

To be honest, I strongly think renormalizing in the metric is methodologically wrong because this way the metric is not measuring the model prediction anymore. The model should take care of it's own predictions (i.e. make them sum to 1), not the metric!
A metric is like a measuring device, say a scale (for measuring weight). We are measuring objects for a flight transport, so lighter is better. Renormalization is like measuring the weight of objects with their packaging removed. But the flight will have to carry the whole objects, with packaging included.
[5] We could almost raise an error if the probabilities do not sum to one (or close), but I feel like it is simpler to just renormalize and compute the loss.

I would be fine with raising a warning first and an error in the future.
[6] I agree with @lorentzenchr that the current behavior is very surprising and therefore it's a bug to me.
[7] What should be the behavior for larger eps values? For example, the following has eps=0.1:
from sklearn.metrics import log_loss
import numpy as np

y_true = [0, 1, 2]
y_pred = [[0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]]

eps = 0.1
log_loss(y_true, y_pred, eps=eps)
# 0.9330788879075577

# `log_loss` will use a clipped `y_pred` for computing the log loss:
np.clip(y_pred, eps, 1 - eps)
# array([[0.1, 0.1, 0.9],
#        [0.1, 0.9, 0.1],
#        [0.1, 0.1, 0.9]])
We could just validate the input, i.e. np.isclose(y_pred.sum(axis=1), 1.0), but log_loss will use the clipped version for computation. For reference, here is the clipping:

  
    
      scikit-learn/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py
    
    
        Lines 2629 to 2630
      in
      d52e946
    
  
  
    

        
          
           # Clipping 
        

        
          
           y_pred = np.clip(y_pred, eps, 1 - eps) 
        
    
  


For me, I think that eps shouldn't be a parameter and should always be np.finfo(y_pred.dtype).eps. For reference, PyTorch's binary_cross_entropy clips the log to -100 by default
[8] I agree with @thomasjpfan that eps should not be a parameter. In my opinion, the perfect default value is 0 (what is the use case of having it in the first place?). I'm also fine with np.finfo(y_pred.dtype).eps.
[9] @lorentzenchr Would it be okay for me to work on this issue?
[10] @OmarManzoor If the solution is clear to you, then yes.
[11] @OmarManzoor If the solution is clear to you, then yes.

From what I can understand we need to raise a warning if y_pred does not sum to 1 and we need to remove eps as a parameter to this metric and instead use a value of np.finfo(y_pred.dtype).eps.
[12] @OmarManzoor Yes. You are very welcome to go ahead, open a PR and link it with this issue. Keep in mind that eps needs a a deprecation cycle, i.e. throw a warning when set for 2 releases. Be prepared that a few concerns might be raised during review.

Title: Choose first feature to use in Tree and/or choose the order of features to use in the Tree
State: OPEN
Author: Dylan-Cunningham
Comments: 11
Body: The idea: Allow a user to pre-select which feature to first split off of and/or allow a user to pre-select which order of the features to split off of.
First example: I might want to first split on a seasonal feature. So, the model would be forced to split on that feature first, and optimize entropy/gini from there. (I am not telling the tree which value to split off of, just which feature to use.)
Second example: I might want to force the model to use 5 features in a specific order. The model would be forced to optimize entropy/gini in the order I specify.
Third example: I might want to force the model to use 3 features in a specific order, but I might pass 10 features to the model. The model would be forced to use the first 3, in the order I specify, then the model could use which other features necessary as specified by the other params.
The story: In finance/trading, sometimes we wish to force which features to make decisions off of (and the order!): all we need is an algo that tells us which levels to trade off of.
We also find it useful to first force a seasonal difference (e.g., winter vs summer), then build a tree from there (one for winter and one for summer). Yes, we could build two trees after first splitting a dataset on our criteria; however, having one model that would do this makes things more succinct. Furthermore, when splitting the dataset like this, the number of rows gets reduced (bad). Mind you, in finance, sometimes it's difficult to get a lot of data.
One might argue that this defeats the purpose of using a model, like a decision tree, which optimizes the levels to trade and chooses which features are more important, but it doesn't. Sometimes optimizing is too prone to overfitting. Plus, the combination of human knowledge (subject matter experts) and data driven models can be better than one, or the other.
If this isn't the best algo or place to suggest this at, I would love some feedback. I would also love to see someone else enhance this idea.
Comments:
[1] This sounds good to combine machine learning tools and expert knowledge on the finance market, and this also enable you more explanation about the whole model. While I'm also afraid this idea may be departure from sklearn itself.
[2] Hi Honfung Wong. Thank you for your quick response. You've mentioned two things, and I'll address both.
I appreciate your opinion about the idea I've presented. I do believe the mix of expert knowledge with ML tools combine to very valuable outcomes.
I have to respectfully disagree with your final statement that sklearn would not be a place for this idea. My idea (which I should/will clarify now) is to implement such logic in the Decision Tree scikit-learn algorithm (and maybe more, if it makes sense).
A decision tree decides which features to split, and splits based on a level in such a way as to optimize entropy/gini recursively, one-by-one. Currently (unless I am mistaken), the DecisionTreeClassifier and DecisionTreeRegressor classifiers do not allow a user to enforce which features must be used, nor the order they must be used, by the algorithm in order to optimize entropy/gini. On the contrary, these classifiers make all the "decisions" for the user.
It is advantageous, in some domains (like finance/trading), to give a user more control, if you will.
[3] I totally understand your opinions and personally I support the new feature, while let me show you something else. Do you know matplotlib.finance, which is used for the visualization of financial data (candlestick)? It was then split out of matplotlib to mpl-finance, and now it has been transferred to mplfinance.
What I wanna say is that, the new features you mentioned above dose make sense (especially for quant) but, I also worry this can cause unnecessary trouble for other users.
I'm looking forward more feedback from the community.
[4] Thanks both for the disucssion. Sounds like LightGBM supports this through forcedsplits_filename.
I think this is something that we might ultimately consider but there are a few technical challenges.
The main obstacle is that we typically don't support feature properties with estimators for now, but this is something we are actively working on. i) we are discussing new kinds of input data, where passing feature information like this one would be more natural than with pure numpy arrays. And ii) we're also developing new estimators (i.e. the histogram-based gradient boosting trees) that now accept a feature-aligned argument for monotonic constraints, and that will hopefully soon also accept categorical feature masks. The forced-splits parameter would be of a similar nature. But these estimators are experimental, and the API is subject to change in the future: typically, these parameters would be better suited for the fit method rather than for the __init__ method, but we don't have support for that kind of workflow yet.
[5] Yes, we could build two trees after first splitting a dataset on our criteria; however, having one model that would do this makes things more succinct. Furthermore, when splitting the dataset like this, the number of rows gets reduced (bad)

Just a side question: are you sure about this, i.e. reduced number of samples? As far as I understand, if you force a split on that feature, you'd get 2 subtrees with reduced number of sample as well, just like if you had splitted the data beforehand?
[6] Yes, I def "misspoke" there. The undertone I was getting at is the model would decide where to split on the feature you, as a user, would supply. Splitting will reduce your data no matter if you do it inside or outside the algo.
[7] There's actually a variant of Decision Tree called Fern that does something very similar. A fern is a restricted binary decision tree such that at each level, the splitting criteria (feature and splitting point) is identical across all nodes on that level. I included an illustration below:

Here's the link to the paper that discusses this algorithm: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1202.1121.pdf
A bagging of ferns achieves competitive performance to Random Forest, as far as I know. I'm looking to modify the DecisionTree class to make a Fern. Is such a hack possible with scikit-learn?
[8] The technical challenges of passing metadata (sample of feature metadata) are now solved. So in principle, this could move forward. But I'm not sure if it's on our list of priorities.
@lorentzenchr might have a better idea about this.
[9] @mayer79 Do you have insights or an expert opinion here?
While I have seen strong use cases for interaction constraints, I do not see or understand the use case here?
[10] @lorentzenchr In LightGBM, there is the option of using forced splits:

path to a .json file that specifies splits to force at the top of every decision tree before best-first learning commences

I think there are indeed a couple of interesting use cases, e.g., in insurance pricing:

Dataset with private cars and commercial cars. Important features like driver age are available only for private cars. In this case, it would be nice to specify: "Please first split on the "private/commercial" dummy feature, not on "driver age" (missing yes/no)", especially when thinking about model interpretability (variable importance, SHAP).
Dataset with (small) vans and (large) trucks. Here, splitting first on van (yes/no) dummy instead on "weight" might bring the necessary logic into the model.

I think in both cases, such an option avoids having to build and maintain two separate models.
[11] Is there any recommended way to model this manually using a custom estimator, until there is any conclusive decision if this will be invited in scikit-learn?
